text:
sam: Heads-up — I ran an nsys capture while chasing a perf regression and the kernel timeline looks weird: at ~500ms we flip from a fast fused-attn kernel to a much slower fallback and KV-cache eviction kernels spike. Anyone seen this pattern before?

maria: Ugh. That usually means the kernel selector moved to the small-seq / fallback path. Did batch size or max-seq change?

sam: No code change in selector, but we did push a batching heuristic tweak yesterday (target_batch_ms lowered). Repro is with batch=4, seq=384.

kevin: Can you paste the nsys capture flags you used? We need the NVTX brackets to see where the runtime switched kernels.

sam: I used:```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o kvcache_triage --capture-range=nvtx --duration=45 --sample=none --force-overwrite --stats true --capture-control=process
```
Not ideal maybe — I tried to keep the capture small.

olivia: Two quick notes: 1) use --sample=cpu or --sample=all when you want call stacks for host-side heuristics, 2) increase duration a bit so sampling sees enough iterations. Sampling=none gives you the timeline but no stack sampling to prove why selector triggered.

perf-bot: Recommend capture command variant for reproducing kernel switching:
```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o kvcache_switch --capture-range=nvtx --sample=cpu --duration=90 --sample-interval=1000 --force-overwrite
```
This captures NVTX range entry/exit, OS runtime markers and CPU samples at ~1ms interval.

maria: Also wrap the spot where the runtime decides kernel in an NVTX push/pop, e.g. NVTX:KERNEL_SELECT_START / KERNEL_SELECT_END. That way capture-range=nvtx isolates the decision point.

kevin: If we suspect KV evictions, add an NVTX span around cache lookup + eviction too. The timeline should show memcpy/d2h/h2d spikes if eviction forces host bounce.

sam: Good call. I can instrument a debug build with more NVTX and re-run. Any tips for kernel names filtering? The timeline shows long unnamed CUDA kernels (jit names) which makes it hard to see which implementation was used.

olivia: In case of JITed kernels, enable symbolization: use CUDA's nvtx annotations at compile-time or run with the environment that keeps kernels' names (avoid stripping). Also nsys has an option to keep CUDA kernel names in the summary table; open the .qdrep in the UI and sort by "Kernel Name" and "Duration".

kevin: Another tactic: force the selector to choose a known path by setting env flags (e.g., FORCED_KERNEL=fast_fused or SELECTOR_MODE=debug) so we can compare timelines between forced-fast vs default. Diff the two captures.

maria: For batching issues — note that lowering target_batch_ms can shrink batch formation and make per-token kernels pick narrow-width kernels (higher per-token overhead). Try a synthetic run with a fixed batcher config: batch_timeout=50ms and batch_size_min=4 to reproduce exact behavior.

sam: I'll do these steps: add NVTX for selector + KV ops, run with --sample=cpu for ~90s, and force kernel variants as a control. Anything else to catch kernel selection state?

olivia: Capture the environment in the NVTX metadata (dump of env vars) and also record the model config (seq len, kv cache enable flags, quantization mode). That helps map selector heuristics to observed kernels.

kevin: One more micro tip — if the kernel switch happens only after a warmup threshold, use a two-phase capture: small warmup, then clear dynlibs or call cudaDeviceSynchronize and start a second NVTX bracket where you measure steady-state. This avoids conflating JIT compile times with runtime-selection costs.

sam: Makes sense. If I see heavy memcpy around eviction, should I suspect our KV cache eviction policy or underlying allocator fragmentation?

maria: Could be both. Look at GPU memory timeline in the capture: frequent small allocations + frees often correlate with fallback kernels because the runtime disables some optimizations when memory is fragmented. Also check persistent allocations for KV store.

perf-bot: Quick checklist to include in the new capture: ["NVTX for selector and KV ops","--sample=cpu","duration >= 60s","force kernel variants for A/B","capture env + model cfg","pinned memory vs pageable test"]

sam: Great checklist — I'll run it now and post the qdrep.

olivia: When you upload qdrep, add a short note with the exact commands and a small trace pointer (time range) so we can jump to the interesting spot. Also attach the timeline CSV export for kernel tables (nsys export --format CSV).

kevin: If timeline shows the slower kernel corresponds to a particular cuBLAS/cuDNN call, we might need to revise the kernel selection thresholds (seq length thresholds or workspace size triggers). Small change to the heuristic can avoid the fallback for our common seq lengths.

sam: Thanks everyone. I'll run with instrumentation and share results in this thread. :thumbsup:
